introduction-when-simple-networking-brea.core: A single VPC with public and private subnets is simple. At scale, with hundreds of VPCs across accounts and regions plus on-premises links, you need transitive routing hubs, private service access, centralised inspection and visibility, and the flat peering model breaks down.

first_principles.problem: 50 VPCs need to talk to each other and to on-prem, and the peering mesh becomes unmanageable.

analogy.title: A town's roads versus a national motorway network
analogy.story: Local roads work for a village; a country needs motorways and junctions.
analogy.breaks: Roads carry anyone; network paths should be explicitly permitted.

check.q: How many peering connections does a full mesh of 20 VPCs need?

the-limits-of-vpc-peering.core: VPC peering connects two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone with no bandwidth bottleneck, but it's non-transitive (A–B and B–C doesn't give A–C), can't have overlapping CIDRs, can't use the peer's internet or VPN gateway (no edge-to-edge routing), and must be managed pairwise.

first_principles.problem: Traffic from VPC A to VPC C via B fails even though both peerings exist.
derivation: Use peering for **a few VPCs** with heavy traffic.
Update **security groups** (can reference peer SGs in-region).
Move to **Transit Gateway** as count grows.

analogy.title: Private footbridges between neighbouring houses
analogy.story: You can visit your neighbour, but you can't walk through their house to the next street.
analogy.breaks: Footbridges are physical; peering has no throughput cap beyond instance limits.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A and B talk; C still needs its own peering.

code.text:
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-a --peer-vpc-id vpc-b
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-a --destination-cidr-block 10.2.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-123
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-b --destination-cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-123

check.q: Why can't VPC A reach the internet through VPC B's NAT gateway over peering?
check.a: Peering doesn't support edge-to-edge routing through the peer's gateways.

the-solution-aws-transit-gateway-tgw.core: Transit Gateway is a regional hub router: VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect attach to it, and its route tables control which attachments can reach which. It provides transitive routing, segmentation (separate route tables for prod/dev), inter-region peering and centralised egress or inspection.

first_principles.problem: Dozens of VPCs plus on-prem need managed, segmented connectivity.
truths: A hub reduces connections to n.

analogy.title: An airport hub
analogy.story: Every city connects to the hub, and the hub's rules decide which connections are allowed.
analogy.breaks: Airports add travel time; TGW adds a small hop and per-GB processing cost.

example.title: Prod/dev segmentation
flow: Prod and dev can't reach each other

check.q: How does TGW isolate prod from dev while sharing services?
check.a: Separate route tables: prod and dev only propagate to and learn routes from shared services, not each other.

privatelink-part-1-gateway-endpoints.core: Gateway endpoints let VPCs reach S3 and DynamoDB privately by adding a route (prefix list) in route tables. Traffic stays on the AWS network without NAT or internet gateways, is free, and can be restricted with endpoint policies and bucket policies (aws:SourceVpce).

first_principles.problem: Private subnets send terabytes to S3 through a NAT gateway, costing thousands a month.
truths: NAT gateways charge per GB processed.
S3 and DynamoDB support gateway endpoints.
Routes direct traffic to the endpoint.
derivation: Note: **in-region only**, not reachable from on-prem.

analogy.title: A private service road to the warehouse
analogy.story: No toll booth (NAT), no public highway.
analogy.breaks: Service roads can be used by anyone nearby; endpoint policies restrict exactly who and what.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: NAT data-processing charges for S3 drop to zero.

code.text:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-123 --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 \
  --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --route-table-ids rtb-private-a rtb-private-b

check.q: Why do gateway endpoints save money?
check.a: S3/DynamoDB traffic bypasses the NAT gateway, avoiding its per-GB processing charge.

privatelink-part-2-interface-endpoints.core: Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) place ENIs with private IPs in your subnets for AWS services (SQS, KMS, ECR, STS…) or third-party and internal services exposed via a Network Load Balancer. Consumers reach the service privately without routing between VPCs, and overlapping CIDRs don't matter.

first_principles.problem: A team wants to expose an internal API to 200 consumer VPCs without peering or exposing networks.
truths: ENIs give private IPs in the consumer VPC.
Only the service, not the whole network, is exposed.
Private DNS can override public names.
derivation: **AWS services**: create interface endpoints, enable private DNS.
Secure with **security groups** on endpoint ENIs.
Cost: **per hour per AZ + per GB**.

analogy.title: A service hatch in a wall
analogy.story: You can order through the hatch without either side entering the other's building.
analogy.breaks: Hatches are one-way in practice; PrivateLink is consumer-initiated only.

example.title: ECR pulls without NAT
example.scenario: Endpoints for a private EKS cluster.
flow: Interface endpoints: ecr.api, ecr.dkr, sts, logs

check.q: Why does PrivateLink work with overlapping CIDRs?
check.a: Consumers connect to an ENI in their own VPC; there's no routing between the two networks.

seeing-the-invisible-vpc-flow-logs.core: VPC Flow Logs record metadata about IP traffic (source, destination, ports, protocol, bytes, ACCEPT/REJECT) at VPC, subnet or ENI level, delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose. They show who talks to whom, reveal blocked traffic and support security investigations; they don't capture payloads.

first_principles.problem: A connection times out and nobody knows if a security group or NACL is dropping it.
truths: Network traffic is invisible by default.
Metadata is enough for most investigations.

analogy.title: Phone call records without recordings
analogy.story: You know who called whom, when and for how long, not what was said.
analogy.breaks: Phone records are complete; flow logs are aggregated per window and may skip some traffic (e.g. DNS to Route 53 resolver).

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Port 5432 rejected from the app subnet: missing SG rule.

code.text:
SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr, dstport, count(*) AS n
FROM vpc_flow_logs
WHERE action = 'REJECT' AND dstaddr = '10.0.3.25'
GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 20;

check.q: Do flow logs capture packet contents?
check.a: No, only metadata about flows (addresses, ports, bytes, action).

global-accelerator-vs-cloudfront-improvi.core: CloudFront is a CDN: it caches HTTP(S) content at the edge and can accelerate dynamic HTTP. Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs that route TCP/UDP traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge, then to healthy regional endpoints, with fast failover. It doesn't cache.

first_principles.problem: A multiplayer game (UDP) and a static website both want lower global latency.
truths: Caching only helps cacheable HTTP content.
derivation: **Global Accelerator** for TCP/UDP, static IPs, fast regional failover.
**Both** use edge locations and the AWS backbone.

analogy.title: A local shop stocking items versus an express lane onto the motorway
analogy.story: The shop serves popular items locally; the express lane gets you to the distant store faster.
analogy.breaks: Express lanes help everyone; GA helps only traffic you route through its IPs.

example.title: Choosing per workload
flow: UDP game servers in 3 regions → Global Accelerator
Partner needs fixed IPs → Global Accelerator

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each workload gets the right acceleration.

check.q: When would you choose Global Accelerator over CloudFront?
check.a: For non-HTTP (TCP/UDP) traffic, static anycast IPs, or fast cross-region failover without caching.
